title: Rereading chapters 13–16
hookLine: reread the world, the Buddha, happiness, pleasure
tomorrow: what does a silversmith's breath have to do with getting better?

cards: Somebody at dinner says it out loud: if you never get attached, you never get hurt. Half the table nods. The other half looks horrified.
The Dhammapada seems to take a side. In the chapter Max Müller calls pleasure: “Let, therefore, no man love anything; loss of the beloved is evil.”
But a few pages earlier, the chapter on happiness sings: “Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us!” Love nothing, or live happily. Readers in the tradition have taken this two ways.

teach.h: READING ONE: LOOSEN THE GRIP ON ALL.
teach.b: The first reading takes the verse at its word. The same chapter goes on: from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; whoever is free of it knows neither.
Readers who hold this view point out that the Buddha left home, and that monks and nuns still leave home to follow him.
Everything loved will one day be lost, so the way out of grief is to loosen the grip on everything, people included. Its best case: it's honest. Nobody keeps anyone forever.

teach.h: READING TWO: PIYA, WHAT I HOLD AS MINE.
teach.b: The second reading starts from the chapter's Pali name, piya, which means dear: what a person holds as mine.
Readers who hold this view point back to the happiness chapter, which praises trust as the best of relationships and the wise as company like meeting with family.
Elsewhere the Buddha teaches loving-kindness toward every being. So the trouble is the clinging, not the warmth. Its best case: it fits the whole book, not one verse.
Notice what the two readings share.
Neither says grief proves you loved wrong. Both say the happiness the book is after doesn't depend on keeping what you love.
And the chapter on the world, between them, gives a picture of change: someone who was careless and then turned around brightens this world like the moon freed from clouds.
Happier now, on a reread, might be exactly that: the same people, held more lightly.

how: Theravada monks and nuns leave home and family life, while lay Buddhists keep families and practice loving-kindness toward them; teachers in both settings read the chapter on what is dear as a warning about clinging.

games.q: your friend says the verse means: never get attached to anyone, ever. what's the best case for her side?
o: nobody keeps anyone forever; loosening the grip spares real grief.
she's scared of commitment and using an old verse as cover.
the verse is badly translated, so her reading can't stand.
games.why: that's her reading at its strongest, and it's honest. the other reading agrees about the grip and keeps the warmth.

practice: Count the people and things that are dear to you, one finger for each, slowly. With each one, let your hand open a little, the way you'd hold a small bird rather than a rope.
When you run out of fingers, start again, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Rereading chapters 13 to 16: the world, the Buddha, happiness and pleasure, read again. Two readings of one hard verse, and what they share.

orig.note: Pali: dear, beloved; the sixteenth chapter is the Piyavagga, which Müller titles 'Pleasure'.

carryVoice: For the road: happier now, holding dear things a little more lightly. That's four of seven, reread.
